prize_parts.citation: for showing how firm heterogeneity and selection into exporting reshape the gains from trade

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged from round 1: B048 with Melitz and Helpman as a single two-name part. My opening first choice was B015, and I moved to B048 in round 1. I have used the exchange to test that move rather than just repeat it. B048 identifies a specific mechanism (selection of heterogeneous firms into exporting and reallocation across firms) that generated predictions about exporter premia, selection and within-industry reallocation after liberalisation. These predictions could be checked in firm-level data, and over two decades and many countries the qualitative ones have held. That is the kind of discovery I would reward under common criteria in any field: a clear mechanism, a clear originator, and evidence that has had time to accumulate. Credit divides cleanly. Melitz (2003) is the model, and Helpman's work with Melitz and Yeaple on exporting versus FDI is a direct extension, together with his earlier trade theory. The chair's questions did not change this. If the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum priority issue is judged material, a citation confined to the selection-and-reallocation mechanism handles it without changing my preference. The B048 case does not rest on counts of support, and I do not treat the seven-member convergence as evidence of merit. I treat it as a sign that independent attribution analyses reached the same two names.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still priority and breadth of credit. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum (and Yeaple) developed parallel firm-level facts and models that are outside the ballot entry. A Melitz-Helpman prize could therefore be read as favouring the theory over the empirical foundations, and a three-name cap cannot fix that. Second, welfare-gain magnitudes depend on functional forms such as Pareto productivity, so the evidence is strongest for the qualitative predictions and weaker for the size of the selection gains. As a labour economist I value identification and should not mistake the model's elegance for settled quantitative evidence. Third, Helpman's separate appearance in B026 means the citation should be drawn tightly. Fourth, B001 is a serious rival on field creation, and its supporters make a fair point that critique is part of maturity. I also record that the chair is a B001 supporter. I do not read that as a reason to discount the argument, only as context.

responses.point: Hassler prefers B001 and calls the gap with B048 small. He would word the citation around measurable institutions and the established link between investor protection and financial outcomes, not the strong causal legal-origins reading. He says creating a new field is somewhat more decisive than refinement within one, and he concedes that omitting Vishny is a real attribution cost.
responses.response: The wording he proposes is the most defensible version of B001, and it answers the chair's question about what can be claimed without the strong causal reading. It does make the credited contribution mainly the data, the measurement and the regularities, and the interpretation of those regularities is the part still in dispute. I would hold the prize to the same standard as a quasi-experimental paper, namely what exactly is identified. Under that standard the B048 mechanism is better established than the B001 regularities. On field creation, I think B048 also qualifies. Selection into exporting turned firm-level customs and census data into a standard test bed for trade theory, so it is not just refinement of an established field. I accept that the Vishny cost and the Shleifer boundary problem are tolerable with careful wording. So I keep B001 as my first alternative and I regard the choice as a close one, not a clear-cut one.

responses.point: Friberg prefers B001 with moderate confidence. He concedes it would not compete with B015-type designs on identification, and he rests the case on the field-creating contribution, 25 years of testing and the idea that the critiques show maturity. He lists B048 as his first alternative because of its cleaner two-name attribution.
responses.response: I appreciate that he separates the case for B001 from identification strength, because it lets us compare the candidates on one criterion each. I agree that critique and extension are part of maturity. My concern is narrower: maturity shows the work has been tested, and it does not show the central claim survived. For B048 the qualitative predictions largely survived, while for B001 the causal core was qualified. Because he already ranks B048 as his first alternative, I think the real question for him is whether the Committee should reward field creation when the central interpretation was qualified. I would answer no, but I recognise the answer depends on how heavily one weights influence against robustness. I also agree that B015 fits a committee that puts identification first, and I keep it as an alternative for that reason.

responses.point: Krusell prefers B037 (Kiyotaki, Moore, Gertler), calls Kiyotaki and Moore the unambiguous core, and would accept a two-name version if Gertler's credit is judged too entangled with B040. He treats the overlap with the 2022 prize as a reduction in marginal novelty, not a disqualification, and he admits that identification of collateral channels is weaker than the theory's influence.
responses.response: I agree that Kiyotaki-Moore is a mature, cleanly attributed mechanism and I ranked it fifth in my opening. His concession on identification is the point I weigh most. By his own account, the case rests on conceptual and modelling impact more than on measured evidence for the mechanism. His answer to the chair's question, that a two-name Kiyotaki-Moore version is acceptable, makes B037 cleaner than the three-name version. It still leaves a smaller body of tested evidence than B048. I do not think the 2022 prize disqualifies B037, so I do not use it against the work. For me the gap with B048 is the evidence for the mechanism, not novelty. I do not list B037 among my two alternatives, but a two-name Kiyotaki-Moore prize would be a coherent outcome.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson, who also prefers B048, calls the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum line the real vulnerability because it concerns priority on the empirical foundations. She would draft the citation around the selection mechanism and gains-from-trade framework so it does not overclaim the firm-level facts. She also moved from B001 to B048 after weighing the identification critique.
responses.response: I agree this is the main risk, and it is the answer I would give to the chair's first question. A citation limited to the selection and reallocation mechanism is accurate about what Melitz and Helpman did, and it does not claim the empirical firm-level facts. I changed the wording in round 1 to say 'linking firm-level data to aggregate outcomes', and I now think that phrase leans toward the empirical foundations and invites the priority challenge. So I have narrowed the citation to the mechanism: 'for showing how firm heterogeneity and selection into exporting reshape the gains from trade.' If the committee decides priority requires crediting Bernard, Eaton, Jensen or Kortum, the cap of three names in the configuration cannot accommodate that without dropping Helpman or Melitz. In that case I would reconsider, and I would turn to B001 or B015 only if they fared better on their own attribution problems.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum priority question material enough to change the credit. A mechanism-only citation reduces the problem but does not remove it.
How much the welfare-gain magnitudes depend on functional-form assumptions such as Pareto productivity, and whether that weakens the claim to a robust discovery beyond the qualitative predictions.
How Helpman's separate appearance in B026 affects framing and support for B048.

Whether the committee will weigh B001's field-creating influence above B048's better-tested core predictions. I think B048 should lead, but this is a judgement about weighting, and I treat it as a close call.

Whether B015 can be given a coherent three-name credit given the Katz-versus-Dorn choice, the task-framework lineage outside the ballot, and overlap with the 2023 and 2024 prizes. I rate its identification highly but keep it as an alternative.
All of my assessments rest on my own recollection of these literatures and have not been independently verified.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. None of my documented co-authors or institutional networks (Uppsala/IFAU labour economists, Hessel Oosterbeek and Jan van Ours) includes Melitz or Helpman, the credited names on my preferred part, or the credited names on my alternatives B001 and B015. I disclose again that I am an empirical labour economist who rates B015 highly in my own field, and that my approach favours credible identification, which may bias me toward B048's tested predictions over B001's influence. As in round 1, I have tried to apply the same criteria across fields. The profile also records that I presented the 2021 prize as chair and spoke about natural experiments. That is an attributed institutional statement, not a stated preference on this year's candidates. Conflicts are disclosed and not adjudicated.
